Key Takeaways

SRS Investment Management, a $14 billion firm, added to Roblox and Meta Platforms and opened a new stake in SK hynix in the third quarter, its latest 13F shows.

Roblox is up 10% since Sept. 30, while Meta is down 23% and SK hynix is down 44%.

Analysts' average targets sit far above today's prices for Meta and SK hynix, but Roblox's has fallen by about two-thirds in a year.

Meta is the one the numbers back best: its revenue is still growing 26%, and it trades below its five-year average multiple.

SRS Investment Management, a firm that manages $14 billion, made its three biggest buys of the third quarter in Roblox (RBLX:NYSE), Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) and SK hynix (SKHY:NASDAQ), according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16.

All three trade far below their 52-week highs, and two have fallen hard since the quarter ended. So the question is whether the fund was early, or just wrong.

Roblox needs 2027 to deliver

The fund raised its Roblox stake 50% to 19.65 million shares, worth $833 million at Sept. 30. That's 7.9% of its 13F stocks and its third-largest position. The stock is up 10% since, even though the news has been rough: with its third-quarter results on Oct. 29, Roblox guided to a 10% to 15% drop in fourth-quarter bookings, and its CFO flagged Grand Theft Auto VI as a modest headwind.

Analysts have spent the year cutting. Their average target fell from $146.02 a year ago to $50.39:

Roblox (RBLX): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's just 8% above the last close, and Citi downgraded the stock to Neutral on Nov. 13. To hit analysts' $6.99 billion estimate for 2026 bookings, Roblox needs about $2.0 billion in the fourth quarter, the top of its guide. So the fund is really betting on the roughly 12% growth analysts expect in 2027, with the stock below its five-year average on forward sales.

TIKR tracks 35 analysts on Roblox. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Roblox, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Roblox's Analyst Ratings

Meta's problem is the spending

Meta was the fund's second-biggest add. It raised its stake 24% to 900,781 shares, worth $653 million at Sept. 30, or 6.2% of its 13F stocks. The stock has dropped 23% since.

The ad business is still humming. Third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and management guides the fourth quarter to $73-$76 billion. What's spooking investors is the build: third-quarter capex of $34.9 billion topped operating cash flow of $32.8 billion, and consensus now has free cash flow bottoming at negative $48 billion in 2027. A New Mexico court also ordered a $25 billion penalty on Oct. 21, which Meta plans to appeal.

Key Takeaways

A $6.6 billion fund's three biggest buys of the third quarter were Meta Platforms, US Foods and Burlington Stores, its latest 13F shows.

Analysts' average targets sit 51% above Meta's price and 42% above Burlington's, but only 11% above US Foods, which trades near its high.

Meta's spending now outruns its operating cash flow, and Burlington guided its third quarter below what analysts expected.

At about 17x forward earnings, well below its five-year average, Meta is the one the numbers back best.

Dorsal Capital Management's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows eight stocks it bought or added to. The three biggest were Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), US Foods (USFD:NYSE) and Burlington Stores (BURL:NYSE), and right now they couldn't look much more different.

The firm manages $6.64 billion in all, and its 13F holds $2.86 billion of US stocks across just 20 positions. So each of these three is a real bet.

Meta's ads are still growing fast

The fund added 27% to its Meta stake in the third quarter, ending the quarter with 280,000 shares worth $203 million. That's 7.1% of its 13F stocks and its fourth-largest position. Meta is down 23% since Sept. 30.

Its ad business grew revenue 26% to $64.6 billion in the third quarter, with price per ad up 14%. But Meta's spending has outrun its cash: capex of $34.9 billion topped operating cash flow of $32.8 billion in the quarter, and analysts now have free cash flow bottoming at negative $48 billion in 2027. That's why the stock trades at about 17x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 21.4x.

Analysts' average target has barely moved, from $840 a year ago to $848 now:

Meta Platforms (META): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's 51% above the stock, with targets running from $650 to $1,050.

US Foods keeps winning independent restaurants

US Foods got the biggest add of the three. The fund raised its share count 533% in the third quarter, to 1.90 million shares worth $175 million by Sept. 30, or 6.1% of its 13F stocks. The stock is up 16% since then.

The business has earned that. In its fiscal third quarter, case volume from independent restaurants rose 5.0% while chain volume fell 1.5%, and adjusted EPS jumped 17.8% to $1.26. US Foods also bought back $191 million of stock in the quarter and now guides adjusted EPS growth of 18% to 20% for the year.

title: Sheryl Sandberg steps in to rescue Britain’s $35bn AI hope
detail:
Sheryl Sandberg steps in to rescue Britain’s $35bn AI hope
James Titcomb
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 1:00 AM MST 5 min read
META
OPAI.PVT
UBER
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Josh Payne thought Sheryl Sandberg could help him turn his start-up into a trillion-dollar business

On a Saturday last year, Sheryl Sandberg's phone rang. On the other end was Paul Daversa, a star Silicon Valley recruiter.

Sandberg, Mark Zuckerberg's second-in-command at Meta, had stepped down from the social media giant in 2022 and left its board two years later.

Her public profile had taken a hit after a tell-all memoir by a former Meta executive accused Sandberg and other executives of inappropriate behaviour and creating an intimidating workplace (Meta has denied the claims and pursued legal action). Sandberg had said she did not fancy another big job in business.

Daversa thought he could change her mind. The recruiter had worked with some of the world's biggest tech companies, from OpenAI to Uber. But his client this time was an 18-month-old British start-up run by a 32-year-old former coal miner.

Josh Payne, a former cryptocurrency entrepreneur, had big plans for his data centre company Nscale, and thought Sandberg could help.

A few weeks earlier, he had written down a list of people he thought could turn the company into a trillion-dollar business. Sandberg was at the top.

"You're crazy if you don't jump on the phone with him," Daversa told Sandberg.

Sandberg originally refused, saying: "I don't do boards and I don't do these calls." She said she changed her mind after reading a memo he had sent staff over Christmas. "The only person I'd ever seen write like that was Mark Zuckerberg," she later recalled.

After the two first talked, Payne offered to fly out to California the next day.

Sandberg, 57, has repeatedly drawn comparisons between Zuckerberg and Payne, who is hoping to pull off a flotation in the coming weeks that could value the British company at up to $35bn (£27bn).

"I see in Josh a potentially generationally defining leader," she said in June.

In February, Sandberg joined Nscale's board.

While nominally a non-executive director and rarely seen in the office, she is believed to have taken a hands-on role at the company since then, often talking to Payne multiple times a day.

"I'm spending real time with Josh and his team," she has said. Some employees have taken to calling her "president", according to one insider. Sandberg herself has said Payne runs the company and that she does not plan to join full-time.

Nscale, just two years old, is seeking to go public in the face of tumultuous market conditions that have delayed other stock market listings and sent the share prices of its rivals crashing.

The company is also among those reeling from the downfall of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss and one of its major backers. The blows have led bosses to consider delaying the float.

title: AppLovin vs. Reddit: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

AppLovin vs. Reddit: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Trading disclosure

The digital advertising landscape is shifting as data-driven platforms fight for marketing budgets. Choosing between AppLovin (NASDAQ:APP) and Reddit (NYSE:RDDT) requires weighing a seasoned software powerhouse against a rapidly growing social platform.

AppLovin specializes in ad-tech software that helps developers grow their apps, while Reddit operates a massive network of user-generated communities. Both companies are successfully capitalizing on specialized data to attract advertisers, but they operate with different business models and cost structures.

The case for AppLovin

AppLovin provides a software-based marketing platform and advertising solutions for consumer brands and gaming apps. The company notes that some of its customers are also competitors, such as Meta Platforms, Alphabet, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and Unity Software (NYSE:U). Following the June 2025 divestiture of its Apps business, the company focuses entirely on its high-margin software platform.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $7.6 billion, representing growth of approximately 46.5% compared to the prior period. Net income was roughly $5.0 billion during this time frame, supported by a strong net margin of 65.9%. This performance highlights the company's ability to scale its ad-tech infrastructure efficiently while maintaining significant profitability.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.7x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio was 3.3x, a measure of the ability to pay short-term bills using current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was nearly $3.9 billion.

The case for Reddit

Reddit is establishing itself as a unique player among communication stocks by leveraging its vast array of user-generated communities. The company generates roughly 94% of its revenue from third-party advertisers, though it is expanding into content licensing for AI model training. While it serves a global audience, Reddit faces some customer concentration, with its top ten advertisers accounting for approximately 21% of total revenue.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $3.1 billion, fueled by growth of approximately 62.2%. Net income was close to $991.7 million, marking a significant transition to profitability compared to previous years. The platform continues to focus on increasing user engagement and expanding its data-licensing partnerships to diversify its income streams.

title: Oklo vs. NuScale Power: Which Nuclear Stock Is a Better Buy?
detail:
Oklo vs. NuScale Power: Which Nuclear Stock Is a Better Buy?
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 3:39 PM MST 5 min read
OKLO
SMR
META
EQIX
FANG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

As data centers hunt for power, Oklo (NYSE:OKLO) and NuScale Power (NYSE:SMR) have emerged as two of the most prominent contenders in the nuclear space.

Both companies aim to build smaller reactors that can sit closer to the point of use. Oklo emphasizes fuel recycling and has unique partnerships, while NuScale focuses on a modular design already certified by federal regulators.

Image source: Getty Images.

The case for Oklo

Oklo designs fast-fission power plants intended to serve specialized customers like data centers, industrial factories, and military installations. The company is currently targeting major players like Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Equinix (NASDAQ:EQIX), and Diamondback Energy (NASDAQ:FANG) for long-term power agreements. Because its business model revolves around a few massive potential contracts, customer concentration adds a significant layer of risk to the enterprise.

Oklo does not yet report meaningful revenue, as it has not yet brought its first powerhouses online. As of Sept. 30, it had total cash, cash equivalents, and debt securities of $3.1 billion. For the first nine months of 2026, it recorded a net loss of $123.3 million.

The case for NuScale Power

NuScale Power focuses on small modular reactors designed to be safer and easier to deploy than traditional large-scale nuclear plants. The company relies heavily on an exclusive strategic partnership with ENTRA1 for global sales and development. Key collaborations include work with the Tennessee Valley Authority (NYSE:TVC) and other project engagements.

Like Oklo, NuScale does not report meaningful revenue. It ended the third quarter of 2026 with $1.9 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and investments. For the first nine months of 2026, its net loss sits at $135.2 million.

Risk profile comparison

Oklo faces significant risks due to its lack of commercial operating history and the absence of binding power purchase agreements. The company is developing first-of-a-kind technology that requires complex regulatory approval from both the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Department of Energy. Furthermore, securing a scalable supply of specialized nuclear fuel remains a major hurdle for its future growth and operational success.

NuScale Power faces substantial risks related to ongoing securities class action litigation involving its disclosures about project prospects and competitive advantages. The business depends almost entirely on its partnership with ENTRA1, and any termination of that agreement could be devastating for its commercialization efforts. NuScale may still need to secure significant future capital to reach its commercial delivery targets.

Key Takeaways

A $3.2 billion fund opened new positions in Snowflake, TTM Technologies and Meta Platforms in the third quarter, its 13F shows.

All three stocks have fallen since Sept. 30, from 23% for Meta to 52% for TTM.

Analysts' average price targets are 51% above Meta's price and 216% above TTM's.

Snowflake is the one to buy first because its earnings estimates keep rising while its stock falls.

The third quarter's 13Fs are in, and one of the more interesting ones comes from a fund most investors have never heard of.

Tremblant Capital Group's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows $3.24 billion of US stocks across 62 positions. Its three biggest new positions were Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE), TTM Technologies (TTMI:NASDAQ) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ).

All three have fallen since Sept. 30. (A 13F shows only what a fund held that day, so it can't tell us what the fund paid or whether it still owns the shares.) So are they bargains now?

Snowflake's estimates keep climbing

Snowflake is the biggest of the three: 351,240 shares worth $119 million on Sept. 30, 3.7% of the fund's 13F and its third-largest holding. The stock has dropped 25% since then, even as the business keeps speeding up. Product revenue grew 37% to $1.49 billion in the quarter ended July 31, its third straight quarter of faster growth, and management credits AI products with about half of that acceleration.

Analysts have been raising their numbers all along. They expect normalized EPS to more than triple, from $1.25 in fiscal 2026 to $4.34 in fiscal 2029, and their average price target climbed from $271 a year ago to $432 now:

Snowflake (SNOW): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's 69% above the stock's price, and the stock wouldn't need a higher multiple to get there. On the fiscal 2029 estimate, $432 is about 99x earnings. That's just under today's forward P/E of about 101x and well below the 130x Snowflake has averaged over the past year.

Key Takeaways

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 47 sold Alphabet and 31 bought, and 19 of the sellers added to Meta Platforms in the same quarter.

Stanley Druckenmiller sold out and David Tepper cut his stake 46%, but GQG Partners' $2.37 billion buy was bigger than the three largest sales put together.

Google Cloud revenue grew 103% in the third quarter, more than twice Microsoft's Azure growth, while Alphabet's capital spending rose 114% and its free cash flow turned negative.

With earnings estimates still climbing and the stock at 19x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 22.4x, the buyers have the better case on TIKR's numbers.

Some of Wall Street's best-known investors cut Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) in the third quarter, but the biggest checks went the other way.

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 (funds readers know, or ones with $1 billion or more of US stocks, with quant and index funds left out), 47 sold Alphabet: they sold out or cut their shares by 20% or more. Another 31 bought, with a new stake or 20% or more shares added, and 201 held it at the quarter's end.

The famous names are on the selling side

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office sold all 336,300 of its shares, about $120 million at quarter-end prices, its 13F filed Nov. 16 shows. Alphabet had been 2.8% of its 13F stocks the quarter before. David Tepper's Appaloosa cut its stake 46%, to 1.00 million shares, selling about $290 million of stock. Dan Loeb's Third Point sold 83% of its shares, Seth Klarman's Baupost Group sold 31%, and Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital sold out. And 19 of the 47 sellers added to Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) in the same quarter. That's the stock JPMorgan picked over Alphabet in November.

TIKR tracks 58 analysts on Alphabet. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Alphabet, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Alphabet's Analyst Ratings

The buyers wrote bigger checks

The largest sale came from Chase Coleman's Tiger Global, a firm that manages $78 billion. It sold 42% of its Alphabet shares, about $845 million, but Alphabet is still its No. 6 holding at 5.7% of its 13F stocks. Bill Nygren's Harris Associates, the firm behind the Oakmark funds, and Whale Rock Capital each sold more than $400 million.

On the other side, GQG Partners, which manages $164 billion, went from 63,882 shares to 7.03 million, about $2.37 billion at quarter-end prices. That one buy was bigger than Tiger's, Harris's and Whale Rock's sales put together.
